passage:
My worst interview? Fine, I'll tell it. I'm Francis. Two years ago my résumé said I "led the migration of the billing system". I had helped. I ran tests and wrote some documentation. My manager led it. I told myself everyone polishes, and it's only one word.
The first round went fine. In the second, the panel asked me to walk them through how I planned the timeline and handled disagreements in the team. I started talking, and about a minute in I could hear myself going in circles. One of them asked a follow-up, and I just said, "Actually, I assisted on that project." The room went quiet. I didn't get the job.
Now my résumé says "assisted". The interviews go better, because I can answer every question.

qa.q: What did Francis's résumé say two years ago?
qa.a: It said Francis "led the migration of the billing system".

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the second-round panel asked about planning the timeline?
qa.a: Francis felt panicked and exposed, hearing the answer go in circles about work Francis had not actually led.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the interview, and what did Francis choose?
qa.a: When the follow-up came, Francis admitted, "Actually, I assisted on that project", choosing honesty even though the room went quiet.

qa.q: How might the interview panel have seen Francis's answers?
qa.a: The panel likely noticed the circling answers and then the correction, and may have started doubting the rest of the résumé.

grounding: A young professional recalls turning assisted work into led work on a résumé, until interview questions exposed what could not be done.

passage:
I'm Sabina, and I sat beside Jyoti at the client pitch on Friday. Her slides said she had "designed and led" the school-lunch campaign. I remember that campaign. Our senior did the strategy; Jyoti made the posters and handled printing, and she did that part brilliantly.
The client liked the slides. Then their manager asked, "How did you choose which districts to start in?" Jyoti smiled, said, "We used data," and paused. The manager waited. I saw her hand tighten on the clicker. I stepped in and explained the survey our senior had run.
Afterwards Jyoti didn't meet my eyes. In the lift she said, "Everyone makes it sound bigger." I don't know if she believed that. She was very quiet for the rest of the day.

qa.q: What did Jyoti's slides say she had done?
qa.a: Her slides said she had "designed and led" the school-lunch campaign.

qa.q: What does Jyoti's hand tightening on the clicker suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous and exposed, because she could not answer questions about work she had not led.

qa.q: What could Jyoti put on her slides next time?
qa.a: She could describe her real part, the posters and printing she did brilliantly, and credit the senior for the strategy.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Jyoti's claim?
qa.a: Sabina knows the real story, feels she had to step in to cover the gap, and isn't sure whether Jyoti believes her own excuse.

grounding: A coworker watches a young professional's inflated claim in a pitch fall apart under a simple client question.
